title: Bench Finder: choose the visual world
question: Every bench becomes a picture postcard: the front shows the view from behind the bench, and the postmark is its facing. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Postcard Rack
options.lineage: picture postcards on a spinning rack; Dutch PTT postal graphics
options.thesis: Each bench is a picture postcard of its own view, postmarked with the direction it faces.
options.viewport: Map on the left with markers drawn as small postmarks (a ring plus a facing tick). A vertical rack of postcards on the right: photo fronts with a postmark compass in the corner. On a phone the rack becomes a swipeable stack over the map.
options.risk: Can tip into kitsch souvenir-shop nostalgia if the postal marks are decorative rather than carrying the facing data.

raised.raise: Known facings are postmarked in solid ink. Inferred ones are struck in hairline with their confidence, so uncertainty is visible at a glance.
Vermilion is reserved for the one selected bench. Everything else on the map stays ink and blue.
Every bench carries a printed serial (No. 2196 · Amsterdam) that doubles as its deep-link address.

options.label: Topographic Survey Sheet
options.thesis: The city as a survey sheet: every bench is a surveyed symbol with a bearing tick and a legend entry.
options.viewport: A full-bleed map with a sheet-margin frame and graticule ticks. A legend panel lists benches as numbered symbols, and the detail opens as an inset sheet with the photo and a bearing diagram.
options.risk: The most familiar choice: it sits close to every map app, and photography takes second place to the map.

options.label: Title-Card Wall
options.thesis: Rows of bench photos by what they face (water, street, park), with the focused bench expanding to show its facing.
options.viewport: Horizontal rows titled 'Facing water', 'Evening sun' and 'Quiet squares', with the map behind a toggle.
options.case: Strong on photo-led browsing and 'what it faces', but the map loses its place and people don't recognise benches as a streaming catalogue.
options.risk: Reads like a generic media app, and location becomes secondary.

options.label: Provenance Ribbon
options.thesis: One bench's history as a ribbon of evidence.
options.viewport: A single bench's evidence trail down one column.
options.case: Benches have no custody story; people come for places, not provenance.
options.kept: Solid ink for known facings, hairline for inferred ones.

options.label: Raku Smoke Flash
options.thesis: Soot-black ground with one ember-hot active object.
options.viewport: A dark field with the selected bench glowing ember.
options.case: No link to sitting outdoors, and a dark field fights the photography.
options.kept: Exactly one hot accent, reserved for the active bench.
options.risk: Moody to the point of hiding the photos.

options.label: Teletext Service
options.thesis: Benches as numbered pages keyed by digits.
options.viewport: P100 index of benches by district.
options.case: A bitmap grid can't carry photography, and it's a novelty for this audience.
options.kept: Every bench gets a short address number.

options.label: HyperCard Stack
options.viewport: One card per bench, with dithered photos.
options.case: One-bit dither destroys the photographs, which are the product.
options.kept: Back retraces your exact trail through benches.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A clean modern map app with pins and photo cards, executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: Full-screen map, a search bar on top, and a bottom sheet of bench cards.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from any places app by design.
